questions.challenge_mechanism: The line y = x is a decoy. Every textbook figure that shows a curve and its inverse together shows them crossing on that line, and the rule behind the picture -- a point that a curve shares with its own reflection must be a fixed point -- is true for an increasing function and false for a decreasing one. Because f here is a decreasing bijection of [0, 6] onto itself it must swap the two endpoints: f(0) = 6 and f(6) = 0. The points (0, 6) and (6, 0) therefore lie on the graph of f and are each other's reflections, so each lies on the graph of the inverse as well, and neither is on y = x. A candidate who solves f(x) = x finds the third point and nothing else, and then has to explain an enclosed region that the figure plainly shows twice over.
questions.question:
A function $f$ is defined on the domain $0 \leq x \leq 6$. Its graph consists of the three straight line segments joining $(0,\,6)$ to $(2,\,3)$, $(2,\,3)$ to $(4,\,2)$ and $(4,\,2)$ to $(6,\,0)$, as shown in the figure.

Because $f$ is decreasing throughout its domain it has an inverse function $f^{-1}$, also defined on $0 \leq x \leq 6$. The graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the line $y = x$, and it is drawn dashed in the figure.

(a) Write down the coordinates of two points at which the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ intersect, and explain why the two graphs must intersect there.

(b) Find the coordinates of the third point of intersection.

(c) The two graphs enclose two separate regions. Explain why those two regions have equal areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the coordinates of two points of intersection of the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$, and explain why the graphs must meet there.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the third point at which the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ intersect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two regions enclosed between the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ have equal areas.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The function is decreasing and maps $[0,\,6]$ onto $[0,\,6]$, so it takes its greatest value at the left end of the domain and its least at the right: $f(0) = 6$ and $f(6) = 0$ **(M1)**. Hence $(0,\,6)$ and $(6,\,0)$ both lie on the graph of $y = f(x)$. The graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of that graph in $y = x$, and the reflection of $(0,\,6)$ is $(6,\,0)$; so $(6,\,0)$ lies on the graph of the inverse, and it also lies on the graph of $f$. Equivalently $f^{-1}(0) = 6$ and $f^{-1}(6) = 0$. Both points are therefore intersections, and neither lies on $y = x$ **(A1)**.

**(b)** A fixed point of $f$ is a point of intersection on $y = x$, so solve $f(x) = x$ on each segment. On $0 \leq x \leq 2$, $f(x) = 6 - \tfrac{3}{2}x$, giving $6 - \tfrac{3}{2}x = x$, so $x = 2.4$, which is not in $[0,\,2]$. On $2 \leq x \leq 4$, $f(x) = 4 - \tfrac{1}{2}x$, giving $4 - \tfrac{1}{2}x = x$, so $x = \tfrac{8}{3}$ **(M1)**, which does lie in $[2,\,4]$. On $4 \leq x \leq 6$, $f(x) = 6 - x$, giving $x = 3$, which is not in $[4,\,6]$. The only fixed point is therefore $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ **(A1)**.

**(c)** Reflection in $y = x$ exchanges the two graphs: it maps the graph of $f$ onto the graph of $f^{-1}$ and the graph of $f^{-1}$ onto the graph of $f$ **(M1)**. The boundary of the first region consists of the arc of $f$ from $(0,\,6)$ to $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ together with the arc of $f^{-1}$ running back; reflecting it gives the arc of $f^{-1}$ from $(6,\,0)$ to $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ together with the arc of $f$ running back, which is exactly the boundary of the second region. A reflection is an isometry and preserves area, so the two regions have equal areas **(A1)**.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for stating $f(0) = 6$ and $f(6) = 0$, which needs the observation that a decreasing bijection of an interval onto itself must exchange the endpoints; (A1) for explaining that the reflection of one of these points is the other, so each lies on both graphs. Accept $f^{-1}(0) = 6$ and $f^{-1}(6) = 0$ as the justification. Do not credit a candidate who merely reads two crossing points off the figure without justifying them: the point of the part is that they must be there.

(b) (M1) for setting $f(x) = x$ on a segment and obtaining a candidate value; (A1) for $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ together with a check that the value lies in the segment it came from. A candidate who obtains $x = 2.4$ or $x = 3$ and fails to reject it earns the method mark only, because the rejection is precisely what makes $8/3$ the answer rather than one of three.

(c) (M1) for identifying the two arcs that bound one region and tracking where the reflection sends them; (A1) for concluding that a reflection preserves area. A candidate who says simply that the figure is symmetric has not yet said which region maps to which, and should be pressed: the symmetry that matters is the symmetry of the pair of curves, not of either curve alone.
questions.explanation:
The item exists because the usual rule of thumb -- a curve meets its reflection on the mirror line -- is a theorem about increasing functions that gets repeated as if it were a fact about all of them. It fails here for a reason that can be stated in one sentence and that a candidate can find without any algebra: a decreasing function that maps $[0,\,6]$ onto $[0,\,6]$ has to send $0$ to $6$ and $6$ to $0$, and those two facts are two points of intersection in their own right. Nothing in the question says the function is decreasing merely to guarantee that an inverse exists; it is decreasing so that the endpoint argument works.

Part (b) then asks for the one point that the usual method does find, and part (c) closes the loop: with three intersections there are two enclosed regions, and a candidate who found only the fixed point has no way to account for the second. The equality of the two areas is not an extra calculation to be performed -- it is the observation that the whole configuration is invariant under the reflection, which sends one region to the other. The figure is load-bearing in a way that figures often are not: it shows the two enclosed regions, and a candidate who has found only one intersection point can see that something is missing before they know what it is.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: the function is given as a piecewise linear graph rather than by a formula, so the candidate reads the endpoints and the segment equations off the figure. Given and asked: the question asks for the two off-diagonal points first and requires a reason why they must exist, rather than asking for the solution set of f(x) = f-inverse(x) in the abstract. Reasoning chain: a third part on the equality of the two enclosed areas is added, which needs the reflection to be applied to a boundary rather than to a point.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Further Mathematics and STEP: the intersections of a decreasing function with its own inverse, and the fact that they need not lie on y = x

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Assume that a curve and its reflection in the line y = x can only meet on that line, solve f(x) = x on each of the three segments, discard the two roots that fall outside their own segments and report a single point of intersection.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The step that breaks is the assumption that every intersection lies on the mirror line. A decreasing bijection of an interval must exchange the two endpoints, and those two endpoint pairs sit off the diagonal, so the fixed-point equation never sees them.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: One point of intersection only, at (8/3, 8/3), obtained by solving f(x) = x and rejecting the other two roots, leaving the second enclosed region visible in the figure with nothing to account for it.

verification.method: Analytic check of every number in the worked answer: the three segment equations, the position of each candidate fixed point relative to its own segment, and the endpoint values of f.
solution_skeleton: Read f(0) = 6 and f(6) = 0 from the decreasing bijection of [0, 6] onto itself.
Observe that (0, 6) reflects to (6, 0), so both points lie on both graphs.
Write the equation of each of the three segments from its two endpoints.
Solve f(x) = x on each segment and test each root against its own interval.
Reflect the boundary of one enclosed region and confirm it becomes the boundary of the other.
Conclude that the two areas are equal because reflection preserves area.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The numbers are chosen so that the local minimum of f is exactly zero. Every area in the question is a half-integer, the arithmetic is a few lines, and the only thing that decides the answer is whether the candidate carries the last quarter of a square unit or rounds it away. Two turning points in the graph of f' invite the answer three; the true count is two, and the second of them is a repeated root rather than a crossing. The item is therefore not a test of integration technique -- there is nothing to integrate -- but of whether a candidate treats a computed value of zero as a value or as a sign that they have made an error.
questions.question:
The figure shows the graph of $y = f'(x)$ for $0 \leq x \leq 9$. It is made up of the three straight line segments joining $(0,\,0)$ to $(3,\,3)$, $(3,\,3)$ to $(6,\,-3)$ and $(6,\,-3)$ to $(9,\,3)$.

It is given that $f(0) = -2.25$.

(a) Show that $f(7.5) = 0$.

(b) Find the exact value of the other solution of the equation $f(x) = 0$ in the interval $0 \leq x \leq 9$.

(c) State the number of distinct solutions of $f(x) = 0$ in $0 \leq x \leq 9$, and explain why the graph of $y = f(x)$ does not cross the $x$-axis at $x = 7.5$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the areas between the graph of $y = f'(x)$ and the $x$-axis, show that $f(7.5) = 0$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of the other solution of $f(x) = 0$ in the interval $0 \leq x \leq 9$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how many distinct solutions $f(x) = 0$ has in $0 \leq x \leq 9$ and explain why the graph of $y = f(x)$ touches rather than crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 7.5$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The area between the graph of $f'$ and the axis from $0$ to $3$ is the triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 3 = 4.5$, and from $3$ to $4.5$, where $f'$ is still positive, it is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 3 = 2.25$. So $f(4.5) = -2.25 + 4.5 + 2.25 = 4.5$ **(M1)**. From $4.5$ to $6$ the signed area is $-\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 3 = -2.25$ and from $6$ to $7.5$ it is another $-2.25$, so $f(7.5) = 4.5 - 2.25 - 2.25 = 0$ **(A1)**.

**(b)** On $0 \leq x \leq 3$ the graph of $f'$ is the line $f'(x) = x$, so $f(x) = -2.25 + \tfrac{x^{2}}{2}$ on that interval **(M1)**. Setting $f(x) = 0$ gives $x^{2} = 4.5$, so $x = \sqrt{4.5} = \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 2.12$, which lies in $[0,\,3]$. Since $f' \geq 0$ throughout $[0,\,4.5]$ the function is increasing there and this is the only solution in that interval; on $[4.5,\,7.5]$ the function falls from $4.5$ to $0$ without reaching zero again before the endpoint, and on $[7.5,\,9]$ it rises from $0$. The other solution is therefore $x = \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ **(A1)**.

**(c)** There are two distinct solutions **(A1)**: $x = \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$, where the graph crosses the axis, and $x = 7.5$. At $x = 7.5$ the graph of $f'$ crosses the axis, so $f'(7.5) = 0$ and $x = 7.5$ is a stationary point of $f$; part (a) shows that the value there is exactly $0$. The function is decreasing immediately before $7.5$ and increasing immediately after it, so the graph comes down to the axis, touches it at its minimum and turns back up. It does not cross, the root is a repeated one, and the three roots that two turning points suggest never materialise **(A1)**.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for an area calculation that reaches $f(4.5) = 4.5$; (A1) for the two negative contributions and the conclusion $f(7.5) = 0$. A candidate who rounds the areas to $4.5$, $2$, $-2$, $-2$ and obtains $f(7.5) = 0.5$ has done the right mathematics on the wrong numbers and cannot be credited: the whole part turns on the value being *exactly* zero, and the gradient of the segment is $-2$, so the areas are exact halves and there is nothing to round.

(b) (M1) for identifying $f'(x) = x$ on the first segment and integrating to $-2.25 + \tfrac{x^{2}}{2}$; (A1) for $\tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ together with a statement that it lies in $[0,\,3]$. Decimal $2.12$ is acceptable only if the exact form is also given, since the part says *exact*.

(c) (A1) for the answer two; (A1) for linking $f'(7.5) = 0$ with $f(7.5) = 0$ to conclude that the axis is touched rather than crossed. Credit should not be withheld from a candidate who says the root is repeated instead of using the words touch and cross.
questions.explanation:
This is a question about whether zero is a number. The candidate obtains $f(7.5) = 0$ by adding and subtracting areas that are all exact halves, and the temptation at that point is to treat the result as an indication that the arithmetic has gone wrong, because a stationary point that sits exactly on the axis feels like a coincidence. It is not a coincidence: it is the design. The initial value $-2.25$ is chosen to be exactly the negative of the area accumulated by $x = 4.5$ minus the area given back by $x = 7.5$.

Once $f(7.5) = 0$ is established, the root count follows from the sign of $f'$: the function rises through zero once, reaches a maximum, falls to touch the axis at its minimum, and rises again. The answer two is smaller than the three that two turning points suggest, and the missing root is not missing at all -- it has merged with the stationary point. That is the kind of thing a candidate can check: a sketch of $f$ built from the accumulated area makes the touching obvious, and a candidate who sketches it before answering will not need to be told.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Structure: the areas are chosen so that the minimum is exactly zero rather than merely small, which converts the usual root-counting exercise into a question about a repeated root. Given and asked: the initial value is given as -2.25 and the candidate is asked to show the minimum is zero rather than to estimate it from a sketch. Reasoning chain: a third part asks for the exact value of the crossing root, which requires recovering f'(x) = x on the first segment and integrating, a step the parent form does not need.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level and Gaokao: questions that give the graph of the derivative and ask for the number of roots of the function

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Find where the derivative is zero, note that there are two turning points with the function rising, falling and rising again, and conclude that the graph crosses the axis three times.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The step that breaks is treating the computed value f(7.5) = 0 as an approximation. The areas are exact halves, the minimum sits exactly on the axis, and the second crossing becomes a point of tangency that carries no sign change with it.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Three solutions, obtained by pairing each turning point with a crossing of the axis and treating the stationary value at x = 7.5 as a crossing because the derivative changes sign there.

verification.method: Every area and every root in the answer is checked by direct arithmetic in the validator's own evaluator, including the position of each root relative to the segment it is claimed to lie on.
solution_skeleton: Read the three vertex coordinates of the graph of f' from the figure.
Accumulate the signed area from 0 to 4.5 to obtain f(4.5) = 4.5.
Subtract the two negative contributions to obtain f(7.5) = 0 exactly.
Write f'(x) = x on the first segment and integrate to get f on [0, 3].
Solve for the crossing root and confirm it lies in [0, 3].
Use the sign of f' on each interval to conclude that there are exactly two distinct roots, one of them repeated at x = 7.5.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The standard method -- project the displacement on to the direction vector and take the length of the remainder -- answers a different question. It gives the distance from P to the infinite line, and it is the right answer only when the foot of the perpendicular happens to lie between A and B. Here the parameter comes out at 4/3, so the foot is beyond B and the closest point of the segment is B itself. The constraint that the point must lie on the segment, which is the whole content of the word segment, is the one thing the formula does not know about, and a candidate who has internalised the formula as 'the distance from a point to a line' will not think to check it.
questions.question:
The points $A$, $B$ and $P$ have position vectors

$$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}, \qquad \mathbf{p} = 9\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}.$$

The figure shows the plane containing all three points, with the line through $A$ and $B$ drawn horizontally and the segment $AB$ marked on it.

(a) Show that the point of the line through $A$ and $B$ that is closest to $P$ does not lie on the segment $AB$.

(b) Find the shortest distance from $P$ to the segment $AB$.

(c) A candidate obtains $\sqrt{73/3} \approx 4.93$. State what this value is the distance from $P$ to, and explain why it is not the answer to part (b).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the point of the line through $A$ and $B$ that is closest to $P$ does not lie on the segment $AB$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the shortest distance from $P$ to the segment $AB$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the value $\sqrt{73/3} \approx 4.93$ is the distance from $P$ to, and explain why it is smaller than the answer to part (b) yet is not a possible answer to it.

questions.answer:
**(a)** $\overrightarrow{AB} = 2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP} = 7\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 14 + 12 + 6 = 32$ and $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2} = 4 + 16 + 4 = 24$ **(M1)**. The closest point of the line is $\mathbf{a} + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}$ with $t = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}}{|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2}} = \dfrac{32}{24} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, and since $\tfrac{4}{3} > 1$ that point lies beyond $B$ and therefore outside the segment $AB$ **(A1)**.

**(b)** Because the closest point of the *line* is outside the segment, the closest point of the segment is its nearest endpoint, namely $B$ **(M1)**, and the distance is $|\overrightarrow{BP}| = |5\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}| = \sqrt{25 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3} \approx 5.20$ **(A1)**.

**(c)** $\sqrt{73/3}$ is the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the infinite line through $A$ and $B$: $|\overrightarrow{AP}|^{2} = 49 + 9 + 9 = 67$, and $67 - \dfrac{32^{2}}{24} = 67 - \dfrac{128}{3} = \dfrac{73}{3}$ **(M1)**. It is not the answer to (b) because the foot of that perpendicular is not a point of the segment. A segment is a bounded set, and the closest point of a bounded set need not be where the perpendicular falls: it can be, and here is, an endpoint. The perpendicular distance is smaller because it is measured to a point the segment does not contain, so it is a lower bound that the segment cannot attain **(A1)**.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for the two ingredients of the projection, $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 32$ and $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2} = 24$, however they are obtained; (A1) for $t = \tfrac{4}{3}$ together with the observation that the point corresponding to $t > 1$ lies beyond $B$. The comparison with $1$ is the mark: a candidate who computes $t = \tfrac{4}{3}$ and says nothing about what it means has done the arithmetic and missed the part.

(b) (M1) for recognising that the endpoint is now the closest point; (A1) for $\sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}$. Accept $5.20$.

(c) (M1) for identifying the value as the distance to the line and reproducing the calculation that produces it; (A1) for the point that the segment is bounded so the minimum over the segment is attained at an endpoint. Do not credit 'it is wrong because the foot is outside' without the consequence, which is that the smaller number is unattainable.
questions.explanation:
The formula for the distance from a point to a line is a formula about a line, and nothing in it remembers where the segment ends. That gap is the entire question. The parameter $t$ carries the information -- $0 \leq t \leq 1$ means the foot is on the segment, $t < 0$ means it is before $A$, $t > 1$ means it is beyond $B$ -- and a candidate who computes $t$ only in order to substitute it into a distance formula will never read it.

The two numbers are close enough to be uncomfortable: $4.93$ against $5.20$. That is deliberate. A large discrepancy would give the game away, whereas this one looks like rounding, and a candidate who has not checked $t$ has no reason to prefer the larger of two plausible answers. The right habit is to read the parameter before using it, which is also the right habit in the optimisation questions where a maximum turns out to sit at the end of an interval rather than at a stationary point.

There is a second lesson in the arithmetic itself. Nothing here is difficult: a scalar product, a squared length, and a comparison of one fraction with one integer. What makes the item worth six marks is that the comparison is the whole question, and it is the step a candidate is most likely to skip on the way to a formula they have already memorised. A bank that only ever asks for the perpendicular distance teaches that formula; this one asks whether the formula is the right thing to reach for.

provenance.adaptation: Written against the HL vector bullet directly. The coordinate values are chosen so that the scalar product is 32 and the squared length 24, making the parameter exactly 4/3 -- safely outside the segment but not so far outside that the figure looks obviously wrong -- and so that the two distances, sqrt(27) and sqrt(73/3), differ by only about five per cent.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Project the displacement on to the direction vector, take the length of the perpendicular component, and report that as the shortest distance from the point to the segment.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The constraint that the closest point must lie between A and B is never tested. The projection parameter comes out at 4/3, so the foot of the perpendicular is beyond B and no point of the segment achieves the perpendicular distance.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: sqrt(73/3) = 4.93, the perpendicular distance from P to the infinite line, reported as the distance to the segment because the method produces a number and the number looks like an answer.

verification.method: Every scalar product, squared length and distance quoted in the answer is recomputed, and the two candidate distances are compared to confirm that the perpendicular one is the smaller of the two.
solution_skeleton: Write the displacement vectors AB and AP from the given position vectors.
Evaluate their scalar product and the squared length of AB.
Form the projection parameter t and compare it with 0 and 1.
Conclude that the foot lies beyond B, so the closest point of the segment is B.
Evaluate the length of BP for the required distance.
Recover sqrt(73/3) as the distance to the line and explain why the segment cannot attain it.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.11 Definite integrals, including the analytical approach; SL 5.5 Introduction to integration as anti-differentiation; 2.14 Odd and even functions
questions.subtopic: 5.11 The moment of a region found from its symmetry, without ever knowing the function
questions.challenge_mechanism: The integral looks impossible and is not. The candidate is not given the equation of the curve, so every instinct -- find f, multiply by x, integrate -- is unavailable, and the item is designed so that the instinct is not merely unhelpful but a dead end. The tool that works is a substitution that the candidate is unlikely to reach for: putting x = 4 - u reflects the interval about the axis of symmetry, and because the function is unchanged by that reflection the integral reappears on the right-hand side of its own equation. The answer, twice the area, is then one line away.
questions.question:
The figure shows the graph of a continuous function $f$ on the interval $0 \leq x \leq 4$. The graph is symmetrical about the line $x = 2$; that is,

$$f(2 + u) = f(2 - u) \qquad \text{for every } u \text{ with } 0 \leq u \leq 2.$$

The area of the region between the graph and the $x$-axis is $12$.

Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} x\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

(a) Use the substitution $x = 4 - u$ to show that $I = 48 - I$.

(b) Hence find the value of $I$.

(c) A second function $g$ on $0 \leq x \leq 4$ is symmetrical about the line $x = 3$ and also encloses an area of $12$. Explain why the argument used in part (a) gives no information about $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} x\,g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the substitution $x = 4 - u$, show that $I = 48 - I$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of the definite integral $I$ defined above.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the same argument gives no information about the corresponding integral for a function symmetrical about the line $x = 3$ on the same interval.

questions.answer:
**(a)** With $x = 4 - u$ we have $\mathrm{d}x = -\mathrm{d}u$ and the limits swap, so $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} (4 - u)\,f(4 - u)\,\mathrm{d}u$ **(M1)**. By the symmetry, $f(4 - u) = f(2 + (2 - u)) = f(2 - (2 - u)) = f(u)$, so

$$I = \int_{0}^{4} (4 - u)\,f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u = 4\int_{0}^{4} f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u - \int_{0}^{4} u\,f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u = 4 \times 12 - I = 48 - I \quad **(A1)**.$$

**(b)** $2I = 48$, so $I = 24$ **(M1)** **(A1)**. This is $2 \times 12$: the integral of $x\,f(x)$ over the region is the abscissa of the axis of symmetry multiplied by the area, which is what a centroid argument would also give, since the centroid of a region with a vertical axis of symmetry lies on that axis.

**(c)** The substitution $x = 4 - u$ reflects the interval $[0,\,4]$ about the line $x = 2$, and that reflection maps the interval onto itself **(M1)**. Reflecting $[0,\,4]$ about the line $x = 3$ instead sends it to $[2,\,6]$, which is not the interval the integral runs over, so the substituted integral cannot be renamed as the original one and the symmetry of $g$ produces no relation between the integral and itself. A symmetry is only useful here if it is a symmetry of the interval as well as of the function **(A1)**.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for carrying out the substitution correctly, including the interchange of limits; (A1) for using $f(4 - u) = f(u)$ and separating the integral into $4\int f - I$. The separation is the mark: a candidate who writes the substituted integral and stops has not yet produced an equation in $I$.

(b) (M1) for $2I = 48$; (A1) for $I = 24$.

(c) (M1) for noticing that the reflection is of the interval and not only of the function; (A1) for the conclusion. Credit a candidate who makes the point by remarking that $x = 6 - u$ would be the substitution matching an axis at $x = 3$ and that it turns $[0,\,4]$ into $[2,\,6]$. Watch for the converse error, which is to claim the method still works; it does not, and a candidate who thinks it does has not noticed that the limits moved.
questions.explanation:
The item asks for a quantity that normally requires the function and then withholds the function, which is the signal that the function is not needed. The substitution $x = 4 - u$ is not a technique for evaluating an integral here; it is a way of saying that the region can be paired with itself, strip by strip, and that the pair of strips at $2 + u$ and $2 - u$ contributes $(2 + u)\,f + (2 - u)\,f = 4f$ rather than something that depends on the shape of $f$. Once that is seen, the answer is $2 \times 12$ by inspection.

Part (c) is the part that separates understanding from technique. A candidate who has learned 'use the symmetry' as a procedure will apply it to the axis at $x = 3$ without noticing that the axis has to bisect the interval. It does not here: an axis at $x = 3$ reflects the interval out from under itself. The general statement worth carrying away is that the integral of $x\,f(x)$ over a region is the area times the $x$-coordinate of the centroid, and the centroid sits on an axis of symmetry only when the axis is one about which the whole region -- interval included -- is symmetric.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: the function is given only as a graph with a stated area rather than by a formula, so no anti-derivative exists to fall back on. Given and asked: the substitution is named in the question but the reason it works is not, and the candidate must supply it. Reasoning chain: a third part asks why the same argument fails for an axis that does not bisect the interval, which the parent form never raises.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Further Mathematics and STEP: evaluating a definite integral by exploiting a symmetry of the integrand and the interval together

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Try to recover the equation of the curve from the figure so that x f(x) can be integrated in the usual way, and give up when the shape does not match any standard function.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Nothing in the question supplies f, and nothing needs to. The substitution x = 4 - u reflects the interval onto itself, so the integral reappears on the other side of its own equation and solves for itself; reaching for the equation of the curve hides that pairing.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: 24, obtained by assuming the mean value of x over the interval is the midpoint 2 and multiplying by the area -- the right number, but arrived at by treating x as constant, and it collapses on any region whose axis of symmetry is not the midpoint of the interval.

verification.method: The reasoning is checked against two explicit symmetric test functions whose area on [0, 4] is exactly 12: a constant function and a quadratic in (x - 2). Both must give the same value of the integral.
solution_skeleton: Note that the substitution x = 4 - u reflects the interval [0, 4] onto itself.
Use the stated symmetry to replace f(4 - u) by f(u).
Split the resulting integral into 4 times the area minus I.
Insert the given area 12 and solve the resulting equation for I.
Confirm the value against a test function with the same area.
Check part (c) by observing that reflection about x = 3 sends [0, 4] to [2, 6].
